meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What Is the Difference Between a Misfortune and a Calamity?'?
meta.ogDescription: A French joke about a Bonaparte, in print by 1861. Disraeli's name was attached to it in 1887, six years after his death.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Disraeli — a French joke pinned on him after his death
answer.authorDates: In print by 28 May 1861 · first credited to Disraeli in January 1887
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traces this joke to France: its earliest known appearance is The Leeds Mercury of 28 May 1861, where Napoleon III tells his son that Prince Jérôme Napoléon falling into the Seine would be an ‘accident’ and being helped out again a ‘misfortune’. Disraeli died on 19 April 1881; the first version bearing his name ran in The Dial of Chicago in January 1887, and it used different words — ‘mischance’ against ‘misfortune’. The familiar misfortune/calamity phrasing surfaces only in Wilfrid Meynell’s 1903 anecdote biography, where — worth noticing — the sentence in the headline is asked of Disraeli by an unnamed questioner, not spoken by him.

source.heading: Where the modern wording actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Leeds Mercury, 28 May 1861 — a French anecdote, the Seine, Prince Jérôme Napoléon
D. Appleton and Company, New York, 1903 — page 146

source.excerpt: “What is the difference between a misfortune and a calamity?” — somebody asked a new definition from Disraeli. The questioner, being no literalist, but a man of liberal understanding, got the reply: “Well, if Gladstone fell into the Thames, that would be a misfortune; and if anybody pulled him out, that, I suppose, would be a calamity.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ places the earliest known instance in The Leeds Mercury of 28 May 1861, which presents it as a French story: the Emperor explains to his son that Prince Napoléon tumbling into the Seine would be an accident, and anyone helping him out a misfortune.

The same source records the joke aimed at William Gladstone in the London periodical Truth in November 1880 — by an unnamed Conservative lecturer, while Disraeli was still alive, and with nobody crediting it to him. See the chronology ↗.

The misfortune/calamity wording quoted today appears in Wilfrid Meynell’s 1903 biography, which the Internet Archive has digitised from the D. Appleton first printing — the passage is in the full text ↗, offered without a source of any kind.
Wikiquote ↗ files the line under ‘Sourced but undated’, and its only citation is that same 1903 Meynell page 146 — not a document from Disraeli’s lifetime.
source.cutTag: Wilfrid Meynell, 1903 · an anecdote with no source
source.excerptNote: Two things to note. Meynell attaches no date, no place and no witness to the exchange — it sits in a run of collected table talk, twenty-two years after Disraeli’s death. And the sentence people quote as the quote is the anonymous questioner’s setup, not Disraeli’s line at all.

source.rightsNote: The text is free to reuse: the wording quoted here was published in Wilfrid Meynell’s Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography (D. Appleton and Company, New York, 1903), and the Internet Archive’s scan of that printing is marked not in copyright. Every earlier version in the chain — The Leeds Mercury 1861, Punch 1867, Truth 1880, The Dial 1887 — is likewise long out of copyright. Public domain is a statement about the text, not about the attribution: the words are free, but they are not reliably Disraeli’s.

author.name: Benjamin Disraeli
author.heading: About the man it was pinned on
author.metaLine: 1804–1881 · British Prime Minister, Conservative leader and novelist
author.bio: Benjamin Disraeli rose from novelist and political outsider to lead the Conservative Party and serve twice as Prime Minister — briefly in 1868, then from 1874 to 1880 — and was created 1st Earl of Beaconsfield in 1876. His long duel with the Liberal leader William Ewart Gladstone defined a generation of British politics. His reputation as a wit was so complete that ownerless jokes drifted toward him for decades after his death in 1881; this is one of them.

copyAttribution: Disputed. "What is the difference between a misfortune and a calamity?" — in the story this is the anonymous questioner's line; the reply credited to Benjamin Disraeli is "Well, if Gladstone fell into the Thames, that would be a misfortune; and if anybody pulled him out, that, I suppose, would be a calamity." The joke is an anonymous French anecdote in print by 28 May 1861 (The Leeds Mercury), and was first credited to Disraeli in January 1887, six years after his death. Earliest instance of this wording: Wilfrid Meynell, Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography (New York: D. Appleton and Company, 1903), 146. Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: How the joke found Disraeli
misattribution.intro: This is a floating anecdote — a joke that keeps its shape and swaps its victim. It travelled for decades before anyone thought to hand it to Disraeli, and for another sixteen years after that before it acquired the wording everyone now quotes.

items.why: Nothing from Disraeli’s lifetime — no letter, speech, diary or memoir — records him saying it. Quote Investigator ↗ locates the first ascription to him in The Dial of Chicago in January 1887, six years after his death, and calls that a rather late date providing weak support for the Disraeli connection.

The template is French and twenty-six years older than the Disraeli story. QI’s chronology ↗ follows it through Napoleon III and Prince Jérôme Napoléon, the MP John Bright, a fictional baronet, a tailor named Snippson, a mother-in-law, and eventually David Lloyd George.

The London periodical Truth printed the joke about Gladstone in November 1880, credited only to ‘a lecturer of Conservative tendencies’. Disraeli was alive and in public life at the time, and nobody attached his name to it. Source ↗.
Mencken’s A New Dictionary of Quotations assigned the Disraeli version to about 1867, which is where that date in later reference books comes from. As QI notes ↗, he supplied no citation for it.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought was never Disraeli’s to begin with. It was a French joke about a Bonaparte, restocked with fresh victims for twenty years before it reached Gladstone, and it only reached Disraeli’s name in 1887 and this exact wording in 1903 — the full trail is at Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to him anyway
lead: The attribution is wrong, but it is not random. Disraeli and William Ewart Gladstone genuinely detested each other, and their rivalry structured British politics for a generation. A joke about wishing a man drowned needs a target the audience already dislikes, and by 1880 the British version of that target was Gladstone. Once the joke had found him, Disraeli was the obvious mouth to put it in.

There is a second reason, and it is a backhanded compliment. Disraeli’s reputation for cruelty and polish was so complete that ownerless wit drifted toward him for decades after he died — the same gravitational pull that collects stray epigrams around Mark Twain, Churchill and Wilde. A funny line with no owner tends to end up filed under the most plausible wit in the room.
detailsBody: 28 May 1861 — The Leeds Mercury: accident against misfortune, the Seine, Prince Jérôme Napoléon. The earliest instance Quote Investigator has located.
19 January 1867 — Punch: a dinner-party riddle about the MP John Bright, then about the fictional Sir Bilberry Tunks.
November 1880 — Truth: the first documented version aimed at Gladstone, told by an unnamed Conservative lecturer.
January 1887 — The Dial, Chicago: the first version credited to Disraeli, as Lord Beaconsfield, using mischance and misfortune.
1903 — Wilfrid Meynell’s biography: misfortune and calamity, the Thames, and the wording that survives today.
context.pull: A joke that outlived a prince, an emperor, an MP, a tailor and a mother-in-law before it settled on Disraeli.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest known instance of the joke is The Leeds Mercury, 28 May 1861, presented as a French anecdote in which the Emperor tells the Prince Imperial that Prince Napoleon tumbling into the Seine would be an accident and anyone helping him out a misfortune.

QI states the earliest ascription of the quip to Benjamin Disraeli was printed in 1887, in The Dial of Chicago, using the contrasting words mischance and misfortune, and calls this 'a rather late date' providing 'weak support for the Disraeli connection'.

QI concludes that 'based on current evidence this joke template originated in France' and that 'It is conceivable that Disraeli told this joke about Gladstone but the supporting evidence is weak, and he would have been employing an existing template.'
QI records the November 1880 London periodical Truth printing the jest aimed at William Gladstone, told by an unnamed 'lecturer of Conservative tendencies', using accident and misfortune.
QI cites the 1903 source as 'Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography by Wilfrid Meynell, Quote Page 146, D. Appleton and Company, New York' and quotes the misfortune/calamity version from it.

QI lists the joke's shifting targets as Prince Jerome Napoleon (Plon-Plon), Napoleon III, Mr. Bright, Sir Bilberry, Mr. Snippson, William Gladstone and David Lloyd George, plus a mother-in-law in Max O'Rell's 1883/1884 book; and records Punch of 19 January 1867 using the riddle about Mr. Bright and Sir Bilberry.

QI notes H. L. Mencken's A New Dictionary of Quotations ascribed the line to Disraeli 'c. 1867' but 'provided no supporting citation'; QI's update history records the 28 May 1861 citation being added on 22 August 2018; QI also states Benjamin Disraeli died in 1881.

Wikiquote lists 'If Gladstone fell into the Thames, that would be a misfortune; and if anybody pulled him out, that, I suppose, would be a calamity' under its 'Sourced but undated' section, noting it was 'In response to a man who asked Disraeli "What is the difference between a misfortune and a calamity?"' and citing Wilfrid Meynell, Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography (1903), p. 146.

The Internet Archive item is Wilfrid Meynell's 'Benjamin Disraeli, an unconventional biography', published New York: D. Appleton and Company, 1903, digitised from the University of California Libraries and marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT with a documented 1903 copyright notice.

The full OCR text of Meynell's 1903 biography contains the passage verbatim: '"What is the difference between a misfortune and a calamity?" — somebody asked a new definition from Disraeli. The questioner, being no literalist, but a man of liberal understanding, got the reply: "Well, if Gladstone fell into the Thames, that would be a misfortune; and if anybody pulled him out, that, I suppose, would be a calamity."' — with no date, place or witness attached to it.

Benjamin Disraeli, 1st Earl of Beaconsfield, was born 21 December 1804 and died 19 April 1881; he was a British statesman, Conservative politician and writer who twice served as Prime Minister (1868 and 1874-1880), and was elevated to the peerage in 1876.

Historic UK repeats the line 'If Gladstone fell into the Thames, that would be misfortune; and if anybody pulled him out, that, I suppose, would be a calamity', credits it to Disraeli, and gives no source or date for it.
